lines: The loop you just learned never actually cared that it was looking at an array.
It only ever cared about one thing: a question whose answer flips, once, as you move along some range.
A packing check like this one only behaves if giving it more room never turns a working plan back into a broken one.
Suppose that promise doesn't actually hold. What does the loop do about it?
answer: Nothing. It keeps going exactly as before, and it hands back an answer with exactly the same confidence.
The loop never checks the one assumption its whole correctness proof depends on.

lines: Swap out what the loop is comparing, and the identical machine still runs.
The two ends of the range are now capacities instead of positions, and the middle value is a candidate worth testing, not a slot worth reading.
Here is a question that only looks like the kind this loop can answer: true, then false, then true again twice, then false.
Hand it to the identical loop anyway, and it still finishes, and still reports a position, confidently.
But the very first true position in that list is one the loop never even visits.
Now stretch the identical idea across a continuous range instead of whole numbers.
There's no next number to land on exactly, the way there was a next array slot, so the loop has to settle for a range narrow enough to call close enough.
Ask for twice the precision you had a moment ago.
Does that cost you twice the work?
answer: No. It costs exactly one more pass through the loop.
Each pass cuts whatever is left clean in half, so reaching a target half the previous size only ever needs one more cut.

lines: Write down how many passes that takes, and notice something about the formula: nowhere in it does it say what you were actually testing.
It only cares how far apart the two ends started, and how close is close enough to stop.
Here is the whole pattern, given a name by the researcher who first wrote it down in the early nineteen eighties.
Take any question that only tells you yes or no for a given value, wrap an outer search like this one around it, and you get an algorithm that finds the best value, not just a feasible one.
Even its own inventor was careful to say this isn't always the fastest way to get there — only, often, the best one known.
Up to now, every search in this chapter has leaned on an order that was already sitting there, waiting to be used.
The next question hides its order somewhere less obvious, and the first real job is noticing exactly where.
